import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

# Foundations from pandas Time Series

## Before visual diagnostics, define what time means

**Timestamp → calendar → frequency → alignment → resampling → windows → graphics**

::: {.notes}
Este bloco deve ser inserido antes da seção Data and Time Structure da aula principal. A ideia é preparar a infraestrutura conceitual necessária para interpretar time plots, seasonal plots, lag plots e ACF.

[Sources]
- https://wesmckinney.com/book/time-series
:::

## What can a time coordinate represent?

- **Timestamp:** a specific instant.
- **Fixed period:** a span such as a month or quarter.
- **Interval:** a start and an end.
- **Elapsed time:** distance from an origin.

> The representation must match what the observation actually measures.

::: {.notes}
Use preço de fechamento como exemplo de timestamp e produção mensal como período. Explique que a escolha altera slicing, agregação e labels.

[Sources]
- https://wesmckinney.com/book/time-series
:::

## Fixed-frequency and irregular series

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Fixed frequency

- every 15 seconds;
- hourly;
- business daily;
- monthly.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Irregular

- trades;
- incidents;
- publications;
- event records.
:::
:::

A line can display either, but **lag 1 has a stable duration only under a regular calendar**.

::: {.notes}
Em série irregular, shift(1) significa registro anterior, não necessariamente uma hora anterior.

[Sources]
- https://wesmckinney.com/book/time-series
:::

## Python date and time objects

```{python}
from datetime import date, time, datetime, timedelta

stamp = datetime(2026, 1, 15, 14, 30)
delta = timedelta(days=2, hours=3)
print(stamp)
print(stamp + delta)
```

- `date`: calendar date;
- `time`: time of day;
- `datetime`: date and time;
- `timedelta`: elapsed duration.

::: {.notes}
Timedelta representa diferença, não uma data.

[Sources]
- https://wesmckinney.com/book/time-series
:::

## Parse strings into temporal data

```{python}
raw_dates = pd.Series([
    "2026-01-15", "15/02/2026", "March 20, 2026", "invalid"
])
parsed = pd.to_datetime(
    raw_dates, format="mixed", dayfirst=True, errors="coerce"
)
pd.DataFrame({"raw": raw_dates, "parsed": parsed})
```

`errors="coerce"` exposes failures as missing timestamps. It does not repair their meaning.

::: {.notes}
Discuta ambiguidade entre dia e mês. Prefira formato explícito quando a fonte for estável.

[Sources]
- https://wesmckinney.com/book/time-series
:::

## Format timestamps for communication

```{python}
stamp = pd.Timestamp("2026-01-15 14:30")
print(stamp.strftime("%Y-%m-%d"))
print(stamp.strftime("%d %b %Y, %H:%M"))
```

Formatting changes display, not the underlying temporal value.

::: {.notes}
Diferencie armazenamento e apresentação. Labels dependentes de locale podem variar entre ambientes.

[Sources]
- https://wesmckinney.com/book/time-series
:::

## `DatetimeIndex`: time as an analytical axis

```{python}
idx = pd.date_range("2026-01-01", periods=6, freq="D")
series = pd.Series([72, 74, 73, 77, 78, 76], index=idx, name="value")
print(type(series.index).__name__)
series
```

A timestamp-indexed Series supports temporal slicing, frequency logic, shifting, and resampling.

::: {.notes}
O DatetimeIndex é a estrutura central do pandas para séries indexadas por instantes.

[Sources]
- https://wesmckinney.com/book/time-series
:::

## Temporal slicing

```{python}
series.loc["2026-01-02":"2026-01-05"]
```

```{python}
daily = pd.Series(
    np.arange(90),
    index=pd.date_range("2026-01-01", periods=90, freq="D")
)
daily.loc["2026-02"].head()
```

Partial strings can select meaningful calendar ranges.

::: {.notes}
Reforce a necessidade de índice temporal ordenado.

[Sources]
- https://wesmckinney.com/book/time-series
:::

## Duplicate timestamps require a rule

```{python}
duplicate_time = pd.Series(
    [70, 72, 74, 76],
    index=pd.to_datetime([
        "2026-01-01", "2026-01-02", "2026-01-02", "2026-01-03"
    ])
)
print("unique index:", duplicate_time.index.is_unique)
duplicate_time.groupby(level=0).agg(["mean", "count"])
```

Aggregation resolves duplicates only when the rule is analytically justified.

::: {.notes}
Em preços, mean pode não ser a regra correta. Last, VWAP ou preservação por fonte podem ser alternativas.

[Sources]
- https://wesmckinney.com/book/time-series
:::

## Generate regular date ranges

```{python}
print(pd.date_range("2026-01-01", periods=5, freq="D"))
print(pd.date_range("2026-01-01 00:00", periods=5, freq="15min"))
print(pd.date_range("2026-01-01", periods=5, freq="B"))
```

Frequency aliases encode calendar rules, not merely display labels.

::: {.notes}
D difer de B. Frequências de negócio não incorporam automaticamente todo calendário local de mercado.

[Sources]
- https://wesmckinney.com/book/time-series
:::

## Regularization can introduce missing values

```{python}
irregular = pd.Series(
    [10, 12, 15],
    index=pd.to_datetime(["2026-01-01", "2026-01-03", "2026-01-06"])
)
irregular.asfreq("D")
```

`asfreq` establishes a target calendar. It does not aggregate or justify filling gaps.

::: {.notes}
Compare asfreq com resample. O primeiro expressa frequência; o segundo cria grupos temporais.

[Sources]
- https://wesmckinney.com/book/time-series
:::

## Shift values versus shift timestamps

```{python}
shift_demo = pd.Series(
    [100, 102, 101, 105],
    index=pd.date_range("2026-01-01", periods=4, freq="D")
)
print(shift_demo.shift(1))
print(shift_demo.shift(1, freq="D"))
```

- `shift(1)`: moves values relative to the existing index.
- `shift(1, freq="D")`: moves the timestamps by a calendar offset.

::: {.notes}
Essa distinção é central para retornos, lags e alinhamento.

[Sources]
- https://wesmckinney.com/book/time-series
:::

## Time zones: localize, then convert

```{python}
naive = pd.date_range("2026-01-15 09:00", periods=3, freq="h")
dublin = naive.tz_localize("Europe/Dublin")
utc = dublin.tz_convert("UTC")
print(dublin)
print(utc)
```

- `tz_localize`: attaches a zone to naive timestamps.
- `tz_convert`: represents the same instants in another zone.

::: {.notes}
Não confunda vincular um timezone com converter instantes já timezone-aware.

[Sources]
- https://wesmckinney.com/book/time-series
:::

## UTC and local calendar features

UTC supports consistent storage and cross-region alignment. Local time remains important for:

- hour-of-day behavior;
- market sessions;
- business operations;
- daylight-saving transitions;
- calendar seasonality.

> Derive seasonal coordinates in the calendar relevant to the phenomenon.

::: {.notes}
A recomendação é separar alinhamento temporal de interpretação sazonal.

[Sources]
- https://wesmckinney.com/book/time-series
:::

## Periods represent spans

```{python}
month = pd.Period("2026-01", freq="M")
quarter = pd.Period("2026Q1", freq="Q-DEC")
print(month)
print(month + 2)
print(quarter)
```

Period arithmetic moves across spans according to the declared frequency.

::: {.notes}
Somar dois a uma Period mensal significa avançar dois meses, não segundos.

[Sources]
- https://wesmckinney.com/book/time-series
:::

## Convert between timestamps and periods

```{python}
month_ends = pd.date_range("2026-01-31", periods=4, freq="ME")
periods = month_ends.to_period("M")
print(periods)
print(periods.to_timestamp(how="end"))
```

Converting a period to a timestamp requires a boundary convention.

::: {.notes}
Start ou end afeta labels, joins e comparação temporal.

[Sources]
- https://wesmckinney.com/book/time-series
:::

## Resampling changes frequency

```{python}
hourly = pd.Series(
    np.arange(24, dtype=float),
    index=pd.date_range("2026-01-01", periods=24, freq="h")
)
hourly.resample("6h").agg(["mean", "max"])
```

- **Downsampling:** higher to lower frequency, usually with aggregation.
- **Upsampling:** lower to higher frequency, usually creating gaps before a filling rule.

::: {.notes}
Mean e max respondem perguntas diferentes. A função de agregação pertence à definição do gráfico.

[Sources]
- https://wesmckinney.com/book/time-series
:::

## Interval boundaries matter

```{python}
boundary = pd.Series(
    [1, 2, 3, 4],
    index=pd.to_datetime([
        "2026-01-01 00:00", "2026-01-01 05:59",
        "2026-01-01 06:00", "2026-01-01 11:59"
    ])
)
boundary.resample("6h", closed="left", label="left").sum()
```

`closed` controls interval membership; `label` controls interval naming.

::: {.notes}
Limites temporais são parte da estatística, não apenas detalhe de sintaxe.

[Sources]
- https://wesmckinney.com/book/time-series
:::

## Moving windows summarize local history

```{python}
observed = pd.Series(
    [10, 13, 12, 16, 17, 15, 18],
    index=pd.date_range("2026-01-01", periods=7, freq="D")
)
windows = pd.DataFrame({
    "observed": observed,
    "rolling_mean_3": observed.rolling(3, min_periods=2).mean(),
    "expanding_mean": observed.expanding(min_periods=2).mean(),
    "ewm_mean": observed.ewm(span=3, adjust=False).mean()
})
windows
```

::: {.notes}
Rolling usa memória fixa; expanding acumula desde o começo; EWM reduz pesos gradualmente.

[Sources]
- https://wesmckinney.com/book/time-series
:::

## Smoothers encode different memory

```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.7
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(windows.index, windows["observed"], marker="o", label="Observed")
ax.plot(windows.index, windows["rolling_mean_3"], linewidth=2, label="Rolling mean, 3")
ax.plot(windows.index, windows["ewm_mean"], linewidth=2, label="EWM, span 3")
ax.set(title="Different smoothers encode different memory",
       xlabel="Date", ylabel="Synthetic value")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
Não apresente linha suavizada como dado observado. Janela e span alteram ruído e atraso.

[Sources]
- https://wesmckinney.com/book/time-series
:::

## Bridge to forecasting graphics

The pandas toolkit establishes:

- what time means;
- whether the calendar is regular;
- how observations align;
- how frequency changes;
- which values belong to each interval;
- how local summaries are constructed.

Only then can time plots, seasonal plots, lag plots, and ACF plots be interpreted reliably.

::: {.notes}
Use como transição para o conteúdo principal de gráficos de séries temporais.

[Sources]
- https://wesmckinney.com/book/time-series
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/02-graphics.html
:::

**Synthetic electricity-market data for teaching**

Apresente a aula como investigação visual anterior à modelagem. Declare que os dados foram criados exclusivamente para fins didáticos. Tempo: 2 min.

# Motivation

## The central question

> Which visualizations reveal the temporal structures?

**Time order → pattern → seasonality → relationships → dependence → diagnostic judgment**

::: {.notes}
Explique que um gráfico de série temporal não serve apenas para apresentação. Ele orienta hipóteses sobre tendência, sazonalidade, ciclos, eventos incomuns e dependência serial. Tempo: 2 min.
:::

## Learning objectives

By the end of the lesson, students will be able to:

- represent timestamps, periods, frequency, and series identifiers;
- construct and interpret time plots;
- distinguish trend, seasonality, cycles, and irregular variation;
- use seasonal and seasonal-subseries plots;
- explore relationships with scatterplots and scatterplot matrices;
- create and interpret lag plots and ACF plots;
- distinguish structured series from white noise;
- connect visual evidence to forecasting requirements;
- avoid common visual and temporal reasoning errors.

::: {.notes}
Os objetivos são observáveis: cada estudante deverá produzir um gráfico, apontar evidências e explicitar uma implicação para previsão. Tempo: 2 min.
:::

## Narrative of the lesson

```text
SET UP TIME
    ↓
PLOT THE SERIES
    ↓
IDENTIFY PATTERNS
    ↓
EXPOSE SEASONALITY
    ↓
COMPARE VARIABLES
    ↓
MEASURE SERIAL DEPENDENCE
    ↓
FORM FORECASTING HYPOTHESES
```

::: {.notes}
Mostre que o processo vai do contexto temporal básico até a dependência serial. Tempo: 2 min.
:::

## Why plotting comes first

A time-series graph can reveal:

- changes in level or direction;
- repeating calendar patterns;
- changing variance;
- unusual observations or gaps;
- relationships with exogenous variables;
- persistence and lag structure;
- possible data-quality or timestamp problems.

::: {.notes}
Enfatize que elementos vistos nos gráficos devem ser considerados na escolha ou avaliação do método de previsão. Um gráfico sugere hipóteses, não prova mecanismos causais. Tempo: 3 min.
:::

# Data and Time Structure

## A synthetic electricity-demand dataset

```{python}
hours = pd.date_range("2026-01-01", periods=24 * 90, freq="h")
t = np.arange(len(hours))
hour = hours.hour.to_numpy()
dow = hours.dayofweek.to_numpy()
day = np.arange(len(hours)) / 24

temperature = 17 + 7 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * (hour - 14) / 24) + 3 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * day / 45)
weekend = dow >= 5
daily_cycle = 9 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * (hour - 7) / 24) + 4 * np.sin(4 * np.pi * (hour - 7) / 24)
weekly_effect = np.where(weekend, -8, 0)
trend = 0.025 * day
noise = rng.normal(0, 2.2, len(hours))
demand = 72 + trend + daily_cycle + weekly_effect + 0.35 * (temperature - 17) ** 2 + noise

ts = pd.DataFrame({
    "timestamp": hours,
    "demand_mw": demand,
    "temperature_c": temperature,
    "is_weekend": weekend
})
ts.loc[450, "demand_mw"] += 28
ts.head(3 )
```

::: {.notes}
Explique os componentes apenas após os alunos observarem os gráficos. Há tendência leve, padrões diário e semanal, relação não linear com temperatura, ruído e uma observação incomum intencional. Tempo: 3 min.
:::

## Observational unit and temporal key

- **Observation:** one hourly market measurement.
- **Time key:** `timestamp`.
- **Target:** `demand_mw`.
- **Covariate:** `temperature_c`.
- **Calendar variable:** `is_weekend`.
- **Declared frequency:** hourly.

```{python}
print(ts.shape)
print(ts.dtypes)
print("unique timestamps:", ts["timestamp"].is_unique)
print("monotonic time:", ts["timestamp"].is_monotonic_increasing)
```

::: {.notes}
A unidade temporal deve ser explícita. Frequência, duplicação e ordenação influenciam todos os gráficos e lags. Tempo: 3 min.
:::

## Index and columns

```{python}
ts_indexed = ts.set_index("timestamp")
print(ts_indexed.index)
print(ts_indexed.columns)
ts_indexed.head(3)
```

A time index makes ordering, slicing, resampling, and lag construction explicit.

::: {.notes}
Diferencie índice estrutural de uma coluna comum. O índice não substitui a necessidade de verificar frequência e unicidade. Tempo: 2 min.
:::

## Timestamp versus Period

```{python}
print(pd.Timestamp("2026-01"))
print(pd.Period("2026-01", freq="M"))
```

- `Timestamp`: an instant in time.
- `Period`: a span associated with a frequency.

::: {.notes}
Um mês pode representar o primeiro instante do mês ou o intervalo mensal completo. Essa distinção importa para labels, agregações e interpretação. Tempo: 3 min.
:::

## Frequency is analytical metadata

```{python}
print("inferred frequency:", pd.infer_freq(ts_indexed.index))
print("expected observations:", len(pd.date_range(
    ts_indexed.index.min(), ts_indexed.index.max(), freq="h"
)))
```

A regular frequency defines what “lag 1,” “season,” and “consecutive” mean.

::: {.notes}
Lag 1 em dados horários significa uma hora apenas se o calendário estiver regular. Tempo: 3 min.
:::

## Detect gaps and duplicate timestamps

```{python}
broken = pd.concat([ts.iloc[:100], ts.iloc[101:110], ts.iloc[[105]]], ignore_index=True)
print("duplicate timestamps:", broken["timestamp"].duplicated().sum())
expected = pd.date_range(broken["timestamp"].min(), broken["timestamp"].max(), freq="h")
missing_timestamps = expected.difference(pd.DatetimeIndex(broken["timestamp"]))
print("missing timestamps:", missing_timestamps.tolist())
```

::: {.notes}
Uma linha unida através de um intervalo ausente pode sugerir continuidade falsa. Verifique o calendário antes de plotar. Tempo: 3 min.
:::

## Reindex to expose missing periods

```{python}
regular = (
    broken.set_index("timestamp")
    .loc[lambda d: ~d.index.duplicated(keep="first")]
    .reindex(expected)
)
regular.loc[regular["demand_mw"].isna()].head()
```

Reindexing makes missing periods explicit; it does not justify interpolation.

::: {.notes}
Diferencie criar a linha ausente no calendário de preencher o valor de demanda. Tempo: 2 min.
:::

## Checkpoint 1: time structure

Which problems can invalidate a time plot or a lag plot?

1. unsorted timestamps;
2. duplicate timestamps;
3. an undeclared frequency;
4. gaps joined by a line;
5. timestamps stored as arbitrary text;
6. aggregation without stating the interval.

::: {.notes}
Resposta: todos podem alterar ou obscurecer a interpretação. Peça um exemplo de consequência para cada item. Tempo: 4 min.
:::

# Time Plots

## Start with a time plot

```{python}
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.8
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(ts["timestamp"], ts["demand_mw"], linewidth=0.8, color="#0072B2")
ax.set(title="Synthetic hourly electricity demand",
       xlabel="Time [1h]", ylabel="Demand (MW)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Consecutive observations are connected to emphasize temporal order.

::: {.notes}
Peça aos estudantes para descreverem evidências sem nomear causas. O gráfico completo revela repetição e possível observação incomum, mas fica visualmente denso. Tempo: 3 min.
:::

## The viewing window changes the story

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{python}
week_view = ts.loc[ts["timestamp"] < ts["timestamp"].min() + pd.Timedelta(days=7)]
```

Short windows expose intraday structure.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{python}
month_daily = ts.set_index("timestamp")["demand_mw"].resample("D").mean()
```

Aggregation exposes slower movement.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Escala temporal e agregação respondem perguntas diferentes. Agregar remove variação horária e pode ocultar picos. Tempo: 3 min.
:::

## Short-window time plot

```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.7
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(week_view["timestamp"], week_view["demand_mw"], marker="o",
        markersize=2.5, linewidth=1.2, color="#0072B2")
ax.set(title="One week reveals the daily demand cycle",
       xlabel="Time [1h]", ylabel="Demand (MW)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
Mostre picos e vales recorrentes dentro do dia. Não confunda repetição visual com explicação causal. Tempo: 3 min.
:::

## Aggregated time plot

```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.7
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(month_daily.index, month_daily, marker="o", color="#009E73")
ax.set(title="Daily mean demand emphasizes slower variation",
       xlabel="Date [1D]", ylabel="Mean demand (MW)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
A resolução diária remove o ciclo intradiário. Compare objetivos: planejamento médio versus gestão de pico. Tempo: 3 min.
:::

## Aggregation function also changes the story

```{python}
daily_summary = ts.set_index("timestamp")["demand_mw"].resample("D").agg(
    daily_mean="mean", daily_max="max", daily_min="min"
)
daily_summary.head()
```
## Aggregation function also changes the story

```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.7
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(daily_summary.index, daily_summary["daily_mean"], label="Mean")
ax.plot(daily_summary.index, daily_summary["daily_max"], label="Maximum")
ax.plot(daily_summary.index, daily_summary["daily_min"], label="Minimum")
ax.set(title="Mean, maximum, and minimum answer different questions",
       xlabel="Date [1D]", ylabel="Demand (MW)")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
Não trate ‘demanda diária’ como uma definição única. O operador de agregação faz parte da pergunta. Tempo: 4 min.
:::

## Missing values and line continuity

```{python}
gap_demo = week_view.copy()
gap_demo.loc[30:38, "demand_mw"] = np.nan
```

```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.5
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(gap_demo["timestamp"], gap_demo["demand_mw"], color="#0072B2")
ax.set(title="Missing observations create a visible discontinuity",
       xlabel="Time [1h]", ylabel="Demand (MW)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
Uma lacuna visível pode ser informativa. Interpolação apenas para estética é inadequada. Tempo: 2 min.
:::

## Highlight unusual observations without deleting them

```{python}
median = ts["demand_mw"].median()
mad = (ts["demand_mw"] - median).abs().median()
ts["robust_score"] = 0.6745 * (ts["demand_mw"] - median) / mad
flagged = ts.loc[ts["robust_score"].abs().gt(4)]
flagged.loc[:, ["timestamp", "demand_mw", "robust_score"]].head()
```

```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.5
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(ts["timestamp"], ts["demand_mw"], linewidth=0.8, color="0.5")
ax.scatter(flagged["timestamp"], flagged["demand_mw"], color="#D55E00", label="Flagged")
ax.set(title="Statistical flags guide investigation",
       xlabel="Time [1h]", ylabel="Demand (MW)")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
A flag não comprova erro. O evento pode ser real, uma mudança operacional ou uma falha de coleta. Tempo: 3 min.
:::

# Time Series Patterns

## Four pattern concepts

| Pattern | Working definition |
|---|---|
| Trend | long-term increase or decrease; not necessarily linear |
| Seasonality | repeating pattern with a fixed, known period |
| Cycle | rise and fall without a fixed, known frequency |
| Irregular | remaining variation not explained by visible structure |

::: {.notes}
A diferença principal entre sazonalidade e ciclo é a periodicidade fixa e conhecida da sazonalidade. Tempo: 4 min.
:::

## Trend is scale-dependent

```{python}
trend_series = pd.Series(50 + 0.03 * np.arange(365) + rng.normal(0, 2, 365),
                         index=pd.date_range("2025-01-01", periods=365))
```

```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.5
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(trend_series.index, trend_series, color="#0072B2", alpha=0.7)
ax.plot(trend_series.rolling(30, center=True).mean(), color="#D55E00", linewidth=2)
ax.set(title="A smoother can reveal long-term direction",
       xlabel="Date", ylabel="Synthetic value")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
A janela de 30 dias é uma escolha analítica. Suavização remove detalhes e introduz perdas nas bordas. Tempo: 3 min.
:::

## Seasonality has a known period

Hourly data may contain several seasonal periods:

- daily: 24 observations;
- weekly: 24 × 7 observations;
- annual: calendar-dependent for hourly data.

A series can contain more than one seasonal pattern.

::: {.notes}
Período é expresso em observações e depende da frequência. Em calendários reais, horário de verão e anos bissextos exigem cuidado. Tempo: 3 min.
:::

## Cycles are not seasons

A cycle:

- may last several years or varying durations;
- does not repeat at a fixed known interval;
- can appear as a trend in a short sample;
- should not be inferred from one rise and fall alone.

::: {.notes}
Destaque dependência da janela observada. Um trecho curto de ciclo pode parecer tendência. Tempo: 2 min.
:::

## Changing variance matters visually

```{python}
level = np.linspace(20, 100, 160)
multiplicative = level * (1 + 0.08 * rng.normal(size=len(level)))
```

```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.5
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2)
axes[0].plot(level, multiplicative, color="#0072B2")
axes[0].set(title="Original scale", xlabel="Time", ylabel="Value")
axes[1].plot(level, np.log(multiplicative), color="#009E73")
axes[1].set(title="Log scale", xlabel="Time", ylabel="log(Value)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
A transformação log pode estabilizar variação proporcional, mas muda a unidade e a interpretação. Só é válida para valores positivos. Tempo: 4 min.
:::

## Checkpoint 2: name the evidence

For each description, choose trend, seasonality, cycle, irregular variation, or insufficient evidence:

1. demand peaks at similar hours every day;
2. a 60-day sample declines continuously;
3. variance grows with the level;
4. peaks recur every seven days;
5. one isolated spike occurs;
6. a multi-year rise and fall has variable duration.

::: {.notes}
A segunda pode ser tendência na amostra, mas ciclo em horizonte maior. Um spike é observação incomum, não um padrão por si só. Tempo: 4 min.
:::

# Seasonal Graphics

## Add seasonal coordinates

```{python}
seasonal = ts.assign(
    date=ts["timestamp"].dt.date,
    hour=ts["timestamp"].dt.hour,
    day_name=ts["timestamp"].dt.day_name(),
    day_of_week=ts["timestamp"].dt.dayofweek,
    week=ts["timestamp"].dt.isocalendar().week.astype(int)
)
seasonal.head(3)
```

::: {.notes}
Variáveis de calendário transformam o tempo em coordenadas sazonais. Preserve sempre o timestamp original. Tempo: 2 min.
:::

## Seasonal plot: one line per day

```{python}
first_14_days = seasonal.loc[seasonal["timestamp"] < seasonal["timestamp"].min() + pd.Timedelta(days=14)]
```

```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
sns.lineplot(data=first_14_days, x="hour", y="demand_mw",
             hue="date", legend=False, palette="viridis", ax=ax)
ax.set(title="Daily seasonal plot of electricity demand",
       xlabel="Hour of day", ylabel="Demand (MW)", xticks=range(0, 24, 3))
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
O eixo deixa de ser data absoluta e passa a ser posição dentro do dia. Compare a forma e a amplitude entre dias. Tempo: 3 min.
:::

## Direct labels versus a crowded legend

With many seasonal lines:

- a legend may become unreadable;
- color should reflect order when possible;
- direct labels can identify selected lines;
- highlighting a few periods can be better than displaying all equally;
- transparency can preserve context without dominating attention.

::: {.notes}
Não use 14 cores categóricas como se cada dia tivesse a mesma importância. Tempo: 2 min.
:::

## Weekly seasonal pattern

```{python}
hourly_profile = seasonal.groupby(
    ["day_of_week", "day_name", "hour"], as_index=False
).agg(mean_demand=("demand_mw", "mean"))
hourly_profile["hour_of_week"] = 24 * hourly_profile["day_of_week"] + hourly_profile["hour"]
```

```{python}
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.8
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(hourly_profile["hour_of_week"], hourly_profile["mean_demand"], color="#0072B2")
ax.set(title="Average weekly demand profile",
       xlabel="Hour of week", ylabel="Mean demand (MW)")
ax.set_xticks(np.arange(12, 168, 24), ["Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri", "Sat", "Sun"])
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
A média semanal resume repetições e pode esconder variação entre semanas. Tempo: 3 min.
:::

## Seasonal subseries plot: design logic

A seasonal-subseries plot:

- places each season in a separate mini time plot;
- shows evolution of the same season across cycles;
- often includes the seasonal mean;
- reveals both seasonal differences and changes through time.

::: {.notes}
Compare com seasonal plot: um sobrepõe ciclos; o outro reúne a mesma temporada. Tempo: 2 min.
:::

## Seasonal subseries plot by hour

```{python}
subseries = seasonal.loc[seasonal["hour"].isin([0, 6, 12, 18])].copy()
subseries["day_index"] = (subseries["timestamp"] - subseries["timestamp"].min()).dt.days
```

```{python}
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.8
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, sharey=True)
for ax, (hour_value, group) in zip(axes, subseries.groupby("hour")):
    ax.plot(group["day_index"], group["demand_mw"], color="0.3", linewidth=0.8)
    ax.axhline(group["demand_mw"].mean(), color="#0072B2", linewidth=2)
    ax.set(title=f"{hour_value:02d}:00", xlabel="Day")
axes[0].set_ylabel("Demand (MW)")
fig.suptitle("Seasonal subseries at selected hours", y=1.03)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
A linha horizontal resume o nível médio da hora. Os painéis mostram evolução e dispersão por hora. Tempo: 4 min.
:::

## A seasonal heatmap

```{python}
heat = seasonal.pivot_table(
    index="day_name", columns="hour", values="demand_mw", aggfunc="mean"
).reindex(["Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday"])
```

```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
sns.heatmap(heat, cmap="viridis", ax=ax)
ax.set(title="Mean demand by weekday and hour",
       xlabel="Hour of day", ylabel="Day of week")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
O heatmap é uma extensão pedagógica para Data Visualization. É eficiente para duas dimensões sazonais, mas a cor é menos precisa que posição. Tempo: 3 min.
:::

## Checkpoint 3: choose a seasonal graphic

Choose between a time plot, seasonal plot, subseries plot, and heatmap:

1. preserve exact chronology;
2. compare daily shapes across two weeks;
3. track 18:00 demand across many days;
4. summarize weekday-by-hour interaction;
5. identify the timestamp of an unusual event.

::: {.notes}
Respostas: time plot, seasonal plot, subseries, heatmap, time plot. Tempo: 4 min.
:::

# Relationships Between Series

## Covariates and exogenous variables

A target series may be accompanied by predictors such as:

- temperature;
- price;
- calendar indicators;
- promotions or policy variables;
- other market series.

A graph can reveal association, nonlinearity, changing relationships, and subgroup structure.

::: {.notes}
Relação visual não garante disponibilidade futura da covariável nem causalidade. Tempo: 3 min.
:::

## Plot both series in time first

```{python}
relationship_week = ts.iloc[:24 * 7].copy()
```

```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.8
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, sharex=True)
axes[0].plot(relationship_week["timestamp"], relationship_week["demand_mw"], color="#0072B2")
axes[0].set(ylabel="Demand (MW)", title="Demand and temperature over the same week")
axes[1].plot(relationship_week["timestamp"], relationship_week["temperature_c"], color="#D55E00")
axes[1].set(xlabel="Time [1h]", ylabel="Temperature (°C)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
Painéis alinhados preservam a escala de cada variável sem eixo duplo. Tempo: 3 min.
:::

## Why dual axes can mislead

Two vertical axes allow arbitrary rescaling. Apparent alignment can change when either axis limit changes.

Prefer:

- aligned panels;
- standardized series with explicit labels;
- index values relative to a baseline;
- direct comparison only when units are compatible.

::: {.notes}
Eixos duplos não são sempre proibidos, mas exigem forte justificativa. Tempo: 2 min.
:::

## Scatterplot: demand versus temperature

```{python}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
sns.scatterplot(data=ts, x="temperature_c", y="demand_mw",
                hue="is_weekend", alpha=0.55, palette="colorblind", ax=ax)
ax.set(title="Demand and temperature show a nonlinear relationship",
       xlabel="Temperature (°C)", ylabel="Demand (MW)")
ax.legend(title="Weekend", frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
A curvatura foi gerada sinteticamente. Hue mostra que calendário pode alterar a relação. Evite resumir tudo por uma única correlação. Tempo: 4 min.
:::

## Correlation can hide nonlinearity

```{python}
print("linear correlation:", ts["temperature_c"].corr(ts["demand_mw"]).round(3))
```

A low linear correlation does not imply absence of a relationship.

::: {.notes}
Correlação mede associação linear. Relações em U podem ter correlação próxima de zero. Tempo: 3 min.
:::

## Scatterplot matrix

```{python}
pairs = ts.assign(
    hour=ts["timestamp"].dt.hour,
    demand_change=ts["demand_mw"].diff()
).loc[:, ["demand_mw", "temperature_c", "hour", "demand_change"]].dropna().sample(350, random_state=42)
```

```{python}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 7
axes = pd.plotting.scatter_matrix(
    pairs, figsize=(9, 7), diagonal="hist", alpha=0.35,
    color="#0072B2", hist_kwds={"bins": 12}
)
plt.suptitle("Scatterplot matrix of selected variables", y=1.02)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
Matriz oferece triagem rápida, mas muitos painéis aumentam carga cognitiva. Use amostra reproduzível para legibilidade. Tempo: 3 min.
:::

## Relationship stability through time

```{python}
ts["month"] = ts["timestamp"].dt.month
monthly_corr = ts.groupby("month").apply(
    lambda g: g["temperature_c"].corr(g["demand_mw"]), include_groups=False
)
monthly_corr
```

Relationships may vary across time, season, or regime.

::: {.notes}
Com apenas três meses sintéticos, trate como diagnóstico, não conclusão robusta. Tempo: 2 min.
:::

# Lag Plots

## A lag is a shifted observation

For lag `k`:

- vertical axis: current value, `y_t`;
- horizontal axis: previous value, `y_{t-k}`;
- points close to the diagonal indicate persistence;
- structures at seasonal lags suggest seasonal dependence.

::: {.notes}
Lag deve ser interpretado em unidades da frequência. Em dados horários, k=24 representa um dia. Tempo: 3 min.
:::

## Construct lagged values safely

```{python}
lagged = ts.sort_values("timestamp").assign(
    lag_1=lambda d: d["demand_mw"].shift(1),
    lag_24=lambda d: d["demand_mw"].shift(24),
    lag_168=lambda d: d["demand_mw"].shift(24 * 7)
)
lagged.loc[:, ["timestamp", "demand_mw", "lag_1", "lag_24", "lag_168"]].head()
```

::: {.notes}
Shift não verifica o calendário sozinho. A série deve estar ordenada e regular. Tempo: 3 min.
:::

## Lag plot at one hour

```{python}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
sns.scatterplot(data=lagged, x="lag_1", y="demand_mw", alpha=0.35, s=24, ax=ax)
lims = [ts["demand_mw"].min(), ts["demand_mw"].max()]
ax.plot(lims, lims, linestyle="--", color="0.5")
ax.set(title="Lag 1: adjacent hours", xlabel="Demand at t − 1 (MW)", ylabel="Demand at t (MW)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
A concentração diagonal indica persistência horária. A linha diagonal é referência, não ajuste. Tempo: 3 min.
:::

## Compare several lags

```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7
lags = [1, 6, 12, 24, 48, 168]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, sharex=True, sharey=True)
for ax, k in zip(axes.flat, lags):
    frame = pd.DataFrame({"current": ts["demand_mw"], "lagged": ts["demand_mw"].shift(k)})
    ax.scatter(frame["lagged"], frame["current"], alpha=0.25, s=12, color="#0072B2")
    ax.set(title=f"lag {k}", xlabel="", ylabel="")
fig.supxlabel("Lagged demand (MW)")
fig.supylabel("Current demand (MW)")
fig.suptitle("Lag plots reveal dependence at different horizons", y=1.02)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
Compare lags curtos, diário e semanal. A força e forma mudam porque o ciclo diário alterna picos e vales. Tempo: 4 min.
:::

## Seasonal color can explain lag structure

```{python}
lag_24_plot = lagged.assign(hour=lagged["timestamp"].dt.hour).dropna(subset=["lag_24"])
```

```{python}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
sns.scatterplot(data=lag_24_plot, x="lag_24", y="demand_mw",
                hue="hour", palette="viridis", alpha=0.55, s=28, ax=ax)
ax.set(title="Lag 24 colored by hour of day",
       xlabel="Demand one day earlier (MW)", ylabel="Current demand (MW)")
ax.legend(title="Hour", bbox_to_anchor=(1.02, 1), frameon=False, ncol=2)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
A cor ordinal ajuda a interpretar grupos sazonais, mas muitas categorias podem sobrecarregar. Tempo: 3 min.
:::

## Checkpoint 4: interpret lag plots

What would you expect for:

1. strong positive lag-1 dependence;
2. daily seasonality in hourly data;
3. peaks followed by troughs at lag 12;
4. independent white noise;
5. a series with trend but no seasonality?

::: {.notes}
Respostas esperadas: diagonal, estrutura forte em 24, relação negativa ou curvada, nuvem sem forma, autocorrelação ampla e lentamente decrescente. Tempo: 4 min.
:::

# Autocorrelation

## From lag plots to a summary coefficient

Autocorrelation at lag `k` measures linear association between `y_t` and `y_{t-k}`.

```math
r_k =
\frac{\sum_{t=k+1}^{T}(y_t-\bar{y})(y_{t-k}-\bar{y})}
{\sum_{t=1}^{T}(y_t-\bar{y})^2}
```

The collection of coefficients is the **autocorrelation function**, or ACF.

::: {.notes}
Explique numerador como covariação defasada e denominador como escala total. ACF resume relação linear, não toda dependência possível. Tempo: 4 min.
:::

## Calculate selected autocorrelations

```{python}
for k in [1, 6, 12, 24, 48, 168]:
    print(k, round(ts["demand_mw"].autocorr(lag=k), 3))
```

::: {.notes}
Compare os valores com os lag plots. O coeficiente reduz cada painel a um número. Tempo: 2 min.
:::

## ACF plot

```{python}
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.8
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
plot_acf(ts["demand_mw"], lags=24 * 8, zero=False,
         bartlett_confint=False, auto_ylims=True, ax=ax)
ax.set(title="Autocorrelation of hourly demand",
       xlabel="Lag [1h]", ylabel="Autocorrelation")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
Procure oscilações diárias e repetição semanal. Os limites padrão são aproximações e não devem ser usados mecanicamente quando a série é fortemente não estacionária ou sazonal. Tempo: 4 min.
:::

## Reading common ACF shapes

- **slow decay:** possible trend or long persistence;
- **repeated peaks:** seasonal dependence;
- **alternating signs:** oscillating dynamics;
- **isolated small spikes:** sampling variability may be sufficient;
- **near-zero coefficients:** behavior compatible with white noise, subject to uncertainty.

::: {.notes}
Fale em evidências compatíveis, não diagnósticos definitivos. Tempo: 3 min.
:::

## Differencing changes what the ACF sees

```{python}
daily_means = ts.set_index("timestamp")["demand_mw"].resample("D").mean()
daily_diff = daily_means.diff().dropna()
```

```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1)
plot_acf(daily_means, lags=30, zero=False, bartlett_confint=False, ax=axes[0])
axes[0].set(title="ACF of daily mean demand", xlabel="Lag [1D]")
plot_acf(daily_diff, lags=30, zero=False, bartlett_confint=False, ax=axes[1])
axes[1].set(title="ACF after first differencing", xlabel="Lag [1D]")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
Diferenciação remove parte da variação de nível, mas pode aumentar ruído e não garante estacionariedade. Tempo: 4 min.
:::

## Multiple seasonalities complicate interpretation

Hourly demand can simultaneously contain:

- adjacent-hour persistence;
- daily seasonality at lag 24;
- weekly seasonality at lag 168;
- changing calendar effects;
- weather-driven variation.

One ACF plot compresses these mechanisms, so combine it with time, seasonal, and covariate plots.

::: {.notes}
A visualização é um sistema de evidências complementares. Tempo: 2 min.
:::

# White Noise

## What is white noise?

A white-noise series has:

- no systematic autocorrelation;
- approximately constant mean and variance under the usual simple definition;
- unpredictable observations from its own past linear structure.

White noise is a benchmark for “no remaining temporal signal.”

::: {.notes}
Não confunda white noise com qualquer série aleatória ou com erros necessariamente normais. Tempo: 3 min.
:::

## Simulate white noise reproducibly

```{python}
white_noise = pd.Series(
    rng.normal(0, 1, 240),
    index=pd.RangeIndex(1, 241),
    name="white_noise"
)
```

```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.5
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(white_noise.index, white_noise, color="#0072B2")
ax.axhline(0, color="0.4", linewidth=1)
ax.set(title="Synthetic white-noise series", xlabel="Observation", ylabel="Value")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
Pergunte se o time plot sozinho prova ausência de autocorrelação. Não prova; precisamos complementar com ACF. Tempo: 3 min.
:::

## ACF of white noise

```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.5
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
plot_acf(white_noise, lags=36, zero=False, bartlett_confint=False, ax=ax)
ax.set(title="ACF of synthetic white noise",
       xlabel="Lag [1 observation]", ylabel="Autocorrelation")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
Coeficientes não serão exatamente zero por variação amostral. Tempo: 3 min.
:::

## Approximate reference bounds

For a white-noise series of length `T`, a common approximate reference is:

```math
\pm \frac{1.96}{\sqrt{T}}
```

```{python}
white_noise_bound = 1.96 / np.sqrt(len(white_noise))
round(white_noise_bound, 3)
```

These are approximate pointwise bounds, not a guarantee that every spike lies inside them.

::: {.notes}
Com muitos lags, alguns excedimentos podem ocorrer por acaso. Evite teste visual mecânico. Tempo: 3 min.
:::

## Time series signal versus white noise

```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1)
plot_acf(ts["demand_mw"], lags=48, zero=False, bartlett_confint=False, ax=axes[0])
axes[0].set(title="Structured demand series", xlabel="Lag [1h]")
plot_acf(white_noise, lags=48, zero=False, bartlett_confint=False, ax=axes[1])
axes[1].set(title="White-noise benchmark", xlabel="Lag [1 observation]")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
Compare padrões persistentes com flutuações ao redor de zero. Os eixos de lag têm unidades diferentes; destaque essa limitação. Tempo: 3 min.
:::

## Checkpoint 5: white-noise reasoning

Which statement is defensible?

1. every ACF spike must equal zero;
2. one spike outside a bound proves predictability;
3. no visible time-plot pattern proves white noise;
4. white noise provides a benchmark for residual diagnostics;
5. normally distributed observations are necessarily white noise.

::: {.notes}
A quarta é a afirmação defensável. Normalidade marginal não implica independência temporal. Tempo: 3 min.
:::

# Integrated Visual Investigation

## The visual investigation protocol

1. validate the time index and frequency;
2. plot the full series;
3. zoom into meaningful windows;
4. compare aggregation functions;
5. identify trend, seasonal, and unusual structures;
6. construct seasonal graphics;
7. inspect covariate relationships;
8. examine lag plots and ACF;
9. record forecasting implications and uncertainties.

::: {.notes}
Esse protocolo é o principal produto reutilizável da aula. Tempo: 3 min.
:::

## Build a compact visual feature table

```{python}
visual_evidence = pd.DataFrame({
    "evidence": [
        "Hourly persistence", "Daily seasonality", "Weekly seasonality",
        "Temperature relationship", "Unusual observation"
    ],
    "visual": [
        "Lag-1 plot and ACF", "Seasonal plot and lag 24",
        "Weekly profile and lag 168", "Scatterplot by weekend",
        "Full time plot with statistical flag"
    ],
    "forecasting_implication": [
        "Represent short-run dependence", "Represent hour-of-day structure",
        "Represent day-of-week structure", "Consider nonlinear covariate effects",
        "Investigate event and robust loss"
    ]
})
visual_evidence
```

::: {.notes}
As implicações são sugestões pedagógicas baseadas nos dados sintéticos, não prescrições universais. Tempo: 3 min.
:::

## Small multiples as a final overview

```{python}
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 7
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2)
axes[0, 0].plot(week_view["timestamp"], week_view["demand_mw"], color="#0072B2")
axes[0, 0].set(title="Time plot", ylabel="Demand (MW)")
sns.scatterplot(data=ts.sample(500, random_state=42), x="temperature_c", y="demand_mw",
                hue="is_weekend", alpha=0.45, legend=False, ax=axes[0, 1])
axes[0, 1].set(title="Covariate relationship", xlabel="Temperature (°C)", ylabel="Demand (MW)")
axes[1, 0].plot(hourly_profile["hour_of_week"], hourly_profile["mean_demand"], color="#009E73")
axes[1, 0].set(title="Weekly seasonal profile", xlabel="Hour of week", ylabel="Mean demand (MW)")
plot_acf(ts["demand_mw"], lags=48, zero=False, bartlett_confint=False, ax=axes[1, 1])
axes[1, 1].set(title="ACF", xlabel="Lag [1h]")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
Cada painel responde uma pergunta diferente. Não reduza o diagnóstico a um único gráfico. Tempo: 4 min.
:::

## What the graphics do not establish

The graphics do not by themselves prove:

- causality;
- structural stability;
- future availability of covariates;
- the correct forecasting model;
- the absence of data leakage;
- out-of-sample forecasting accuracy.

::: {.notes}
Essa limitação protege contra excesso de interpretação. Visualização orienta hipóteses que precisam de validação temporal e avaliação fora da amostra. Tempo: 3 min.
:::

# Practice

## Capstone exercise

Using `ts`, produce a visual diagnostic report that:

1. verifies order, uniqueness, and frequency;
2. presents a full and a zoomed time plot;
3. identifies at least two temporal patterns;
4. uses one seasonal plot and one subseries or heatmap;
5. examines temperature as a covariate;
6. compares lag 1, lag 24, and lag 168;
7. creates an ACF plot;
8. compares the result with white noise;
9. states three forecasting implications;
10. states three limitations.

::: {.notes}
Avalie coerência entre pergunta, gráfico, evidência e implicação. Não avalie apenas estética. Tempo: atividade integradora.
:::

## Suggested solution structure

```python
# 1. Validate temporal structure
# 2. Build calendar features
# 3. Plot chronology at two scales
# 4. Plot seasonal structure
# 5. Plot target-covariate relationship
# 6. Construct lagged values
# 7. Plot ACF
# 8. Record evidence, implications, and limitations
```

A good report explains **why each chart is present**.

::: {.notes}
A solução não precisa reproduzir exatamente os gráficos da aula. Exija justificativa. Tempo: 2 min.
:::

## Assessment rubric

| Dimension | Evidence |
|---|---|
| Time structure | order, uniqueness, frequency, and gaps checked |
| Visual choice | each chart matches a diagnostic question |
| Temporal reasoning | trend, seasonality, cycles, and lags distinguished |
| Statistical care | association, ACF, and bounds interpreted cautiously |
| Communication | titles, axes, units, and encodings are explicit |
| Forecast connection | visual evidence becomes a testable modeling hypothesis |
| Reproducibility | code executes without external downloads |

::: {.notes}
Use a rubrica para feedback formativo. Tempo: 3 min.
:::

# Key Takeaways

## Time-series visualization checklist

- [ ] Is the time index parsed, ordered, unique, and regular?
- [ ] Is frequency explicit in titles or axes?
- [ ] Have full and local windows been inspected?
- [ ] Is aggregation level and function documented?
- [ ] Are trend, seasonality, cycles, and irregularity distinguished?
- [ ] Are seasonal graphics aligned with the correct period?
- [ ] Are covariate relationships checked for nonlinearity and subgroups?
- [ ] Are lag units explicit?
- [ ] Is ACF interpreted together with other plots?
- [ ] Are forecasting implications framed as hypotheses?

::: {.notes}
Transforme em checklist permanente para projetos de previsão. Tempo: 3 min.
:::

## Main conclusions

1. Plot the data before selecting a forecasting method.
2. Time-index quality determines the validity of temporal graphics.
3. Viewing window and aggregation change visible structure.
4. Seasonal plots reorganize time to expose repetition.
5. Scatterplots reveal relationships, but not causality.
6. Lag plots preserve shape; ACF compresses linear dependence.
7. White noise is a benchmark, not a visual certainty.
8. No single chart provides a complete temporal diagnosis.
9. Visual evidence should become explicit, testable forecasting hypotheses.

::: {.notes}
Retome os objetivos e peça que cada aluno cite um gráfico e a pergunta que ele responde. Tempo: 3 min.
:::
